1: In March 1953 a girl of seventeen called Nella Sarno was working six days a week in her uncle's tile yard on the eastern edge of Naples, counting stock and writing out delivery notes in a handwriting that her uncle said was the only educated thing about the business. On Tuesday and Friday evenings she went to a parish hall two streets away where a woman who had danced professionally before the war taught eleven girls for very little money in a room with a concrete floor. The teacher told her in February that she was good enough to be seen by somebody who mattered, and gave her the name of a school in Rome, and an address, and told her to write and to say nothing about the tile yard. Nella wrote the letter over four evenings. It ran to one page. She did mention the tile yard, in the second paragraph, because she could not work out how to describe her days without it, and she said afterward that she had spent a week certain this was the sentence that would finish her. She posted it on the sixth of March, or rather she gave it to the caretaker of the parish hall to post, because the box outside the hall was nearer his route home than hers and he offered. He put it in his coat pocket. He was sixty-one, he had emphysema, and he did not go out again for two days. The box was emptied at seven in the morning and again at four, and the difference between the sixth of March and the eighth of March is, in the end, the whole of this story. Nobody in it ever knew that, including the caretaker, who was not asked about any of this until 1974 and who by then could not have told you which decade he had posted it in.
2: That is the first link, and it changed everything, because the letter went into the box on the eighth of March instead of the sixth. Letters for the school were opened by a woman named Signora Calvi, who read about forty a day, who had been in the job nine years, and who was competent, quick and had a rule: applications from outside Rome went into the second pile unless a recommendation on headed paper came with them. Nella's came with nothing. On the sixth of March Signora Calvi was at her desk. On the eighth she was at home with influenza, and the post was opened for three days by a twenty-four-year-old typist called Marisa Fontana, who had no rule about the second pile because nobody had told her there was one, and who therefore read all forty the same way, which is slowly. She read the paragraph about the tile yard twice. Then she did something that was not her job and that she was mildly afraid of for a week afterward: she wrote four lines on a slip of paper and clipped it to the letter, saying this one was worth a look and that the applicant could plainly write, and she put the letter on top of the first pile rather than in it. She did not sign the slip. She was a typist and she thought signing it would look like an opinion. Signora Calvi came back on the eleventh, found her piles disturbed and said something short about it; Fontana did not explain, and the two of them worked together four more years without it coming up again. Fontana left in 1957, married, moved to Bari, and heard the rest of it in 1993, from a researcher on a telephone, having to be told twice which letter was meant.
3: The letter and its unsigned slip reached a teacher called Ettore Bassi, who was fifty-two, who taught the second-year girls, and who was by then extremely tired of being asked to look at things. He looked at it. He has always been careful to say that he did nothing, and the record supports him: he did not write to Nella, he did not put her name forward, and he did not keep the letter. What he did was mention it. He mentioned it in a corridor on a Thursday afternoon, to nobody in particular, in the way people say things in corridors — that there was a girl in Naples who worked in a tile yard and who could evidently write a letter, and that she was seventeen, which was too old, and that it was a pity. Three people heard him. Two of them have no memory of it at all. Bassi himself, asked about the remark twenty-nine years later, said that he made remarks like that most weeks and that if he had understood that one of them was load- bearing he would have chosen his words better. He also said, and this is the part his students quote, that he had said it was a pity in the tone people use when they mean it is somebody else's problem. He did not think of the girl again. He had four hundred and ten pupils across his career and he could not have picked her name out of a list. The remark took, by his own estimate, about eleven seconds. He was carrying a folder at the time and was on his way to a room he was already late for, and the letter itself he left on a windowsill, which is where it was found two days later by somebody else and put back on the pile it had come from, still with the slip attached.
4: The third person in the corridor was a rehearsal pianist, Vittorio Greco, thirty-one, who worked at the school three mornings a week and elsewhere the rest of the time, and who had a habit everybody who knew him mentions: he repeated things. Not maliciously. He simply had a great many acquaintances and a poor sense of which information belonged to whom, and arrived at dinner tables with whatever he had heard that week. On the evening of the nineteenth of March 1953 he was at a long table in a restaurant off the Via del Babuino, invited by a violinist he barely knew, in a party of eleven or twelve that had formed for reasons nobody has since established. He told the story about the girl in the tile yard between the first and second courses. He told it as a joke against the school — a piece about an institution that could look at a letter like that and file it — and he told it well, because he told everything well, and he got his laugh. He then forgot it permanently. Greco died in 1988. He was interviewed twice about that evening and could remember the restaurant, the violinist and what he ate, and nothing about any girl. He was not being evasive; he was a man who had told several thousand stories. He was also, and this matters, a man nobody had reason to be careful around. He had no authority over anything, he was paid by the morning, and he was therefore in the room for conversations that would have stopped if somebody senior had walked in. Everything he passed on he passed on sideways, from one table to another, and none of it ever went upwards, which is why the chain runs as it does.
5: Four places along that table was a woman of twenty-three who had been in Rome for parts of the previous year and would, within twelve months, become the most recognised face in the world. She was not that yet. What she did at the table is small and can be stated exactly. She asked Greco two questions: which school, and how old the girl was. Then she said a sentence which three people at that table later remembered in almost identical words: that she had been told she was too old at nineteen, and that whoever had decided that had been wrong, and that it had cost her a year. She did not say it as a speech. Two of the three remember her saying it to her plate. Then the table moved on and she turned to the woman on her left and repeated the whole thing — the tile yard, the letter, the school, the age — in the space of perhaps ninety seconds, and that is the entirety of her involvement. She did not write to the school, did not offer money, and did not ask for the girl's name, which it is not clear Greco knew. She was link five of eight, and her contribution was to repeat something to the right person while passing the bread. There is a version of this in which she took an interest, made an enquiry, followed it up, and the thing was arranged by somebody famous doing good quietly. That version is false in every particular. She was twenty-three, she was working, and ninety seconds of dinner talk is what she gave it. What she had, and nobody else at that table had, was a reason to think the age objection was rubbish; she said so once, and that sentence is the only thing that travelled.
6: The woman on her left was Renata Oriani, forty-four, married to a man who manufactured bathroom fittings in Brescia, and she was at that dinner because he was in Rome for four days and she did not like hotel rooms. She was, by every account, a practical and unsentimental woman with no particular interest in ballet. She did two things over the following six weeks. First she wrote to the school, not about Nella, whose name she did not know, but to ask what a year's fees and board came to for a girl from outside Rome, framing it as a general enquiry from a family considering it. She got a figure back on headed paper: a little more than her husband's factory paid a foreman in a year. Second, she told her accountant she wanted that amount paid to the school annually for three years, that she did not want her name on it, and that if it could not be done without her name she would rather not do it. Her accountant, a man named Pozzi, said it could. What she never did, and this is the thing that makes the rest of the story impossible, is establish which girl it was for. She told Pozzi to ask the school to apply it to a student from outside Rome who could not otherwise come. She left the choosing to strangers on purpose. Her husband, who outlived her by six years, was shown the ledger entry in 1982 and said he had no idea what it was and assumed it concerned a nephew. Her own reason, as far as anybody can reconstruct it, had nothing to do with dancing and everything to do with a sentence about somebody being told they were too old at nineteen. She had been taken out of school at thirteen.
7: Pozzi is link seven and he is the reason there is no paper trail. He set the payment up as an annual disbursement from a holding account under a heading that meant nothing — the word he used, which survives in his own ledger, translates roughly as sundry educational — and he did it that way not out of discretion but because that was the heading he used for everything he could not classify. The school's bursar, a man called Fabbri, is link eight, and his part took about ten minutes. He received a payment with an instruction attached, checked that the instruction was not conditional on anything he was not allowed to agree to, and applied it to the only candidate then in front of him who fitted the description, which was a seventeen-year-old from Naples whose letter was sitting on the top of a pile with an unsigned slip clipped to it. He wrote to her on the fourth of May 1953 offering a place with fees and board provided for three years by a benefactor who wished to remain unnamed. It was, as far as he was concerned, an administrative afternoon. He did not connect the money with the letter beyond the fact that both were on his desk. He retired in 1971 and said afterward that he had processed maybe sixty of these and this was the only one anybody ever asked him about. The instruction was renewed in 1954 and 1955 and then stopped, exactly as arranged, and nobody at the school ever queried the ending because nobody there had ever queried the beginning. There are four pieces of paper in this whole chain and no two of them are in the same country. The letter itself was destroyed in a clear-out in 1968.
8: Nella Sarno went to Rome in September 1953 and stayed nine years, and she was, by the assessment of everybody who saw her work, good but not exceptional; she spent most of her career in the corps of a company in Turin and then twenty-six years teaching. She also spent fifty years trying to find out who had paid. She wrote to the school in 1958, 1964, 1971 and 1989. She got as far as Fabbri, who told her honestly he had never known, and then as far as the word in Pozzi's ledger, which she saw a photograph of in 1991 and which told her nothing. She never reached Renata Oriani, who died in 1979 and never once mentioned it, not to her husband and not in a will. She never heard the name Greco or Bassi or Fontana. She never learned about the caretaker's coat pocket, the link the whole thing turns on and the one nobody could ever have found. What she said, in her seventies, was not that she had wanted to repay anybody. She said that she had wanted to be able to say thank you to a person, out loud, once, and that being unable to do that had been a small continuous weight for five decades, and that people who told her the anonymity was a gift had never had to carry it. She did not put it in those words until she was asked directly, and then she said it in about fifteen seconds, changed the subject and would not come back to it. The interviewer noted that she was perfectly composed and that it was the only moment in three hours when she looked at the floor. This story is a work of fiction. Nella, the school, Oriani, Pozzi and every detail in it are invented, created for storytelling and not drawn from any record.
